Original Article

doi: 10.1111/joim.13461 The ﬁrst wave of COVID-19 and concurrent social restrictions were not associated with a negative impact on mental health and psychiatric well-being

Thorvardur Jon Love1,2 , Inga Wessman3, Gauti Kjartan Gislason1, Saemundur Rognvaldsson1,2, Sigrun Thorsteinsdottir1, Gudrun Asta Sigurdardottir1, Asdis Rosa Thordardottir1, Elias Eythorsson2, Tinna Laufey Asgeirsdottir4, Thor Aspelund5, Andri Steinthor Bjornsson3 & Sigurdur Yngvi Kristinsson1,2

From the 1Faculty of Medicine, University of Iceland, Reykjavik, Iceland; 2Department of Medicine, Landspitali University Hospital, Reykjavik, Iceland; 3Faculty of Psychology, University of Iceland, Reykjavik, Iceland; 4Faculty of Economics, University of Iceland, Reykjavik, Iceland; and 5Centre for Public Health Sciences, University of Iceland, Reykjavik, Iceland

[Correction added on 04 May, 2022 after online publication: The afﬁliations were updated.]

Abstract. Love TJ, Wessman I, Gislason GK, Rognvaldsson S, Thorsteinsdottir S, Sigurdardottir GA, et al. The ﬁrst wave of COVID-19 and concurrent social restrictions were not associated with a negative impact on mental health and psychiatric well-being. J Intern Med. 2022;291:837–848.

Background. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID- 19) pandemic and efforts to contain it have sub-stantially affected the daily lives of most of the world’s population.

Objective. We describe the impact of the ﬁrst COVID- 19 wave and associated social restrictions on the mental health of a large adult population.

Methods. We performed a cohort study nested in a prospective randomized clinical trial, comparing responses during the ﬁrst COVID-19 wave to previous responses. We calculated the odds ratio (OR) of the population moving up one severity category on validated instruments used to measure stress (PSS-10), anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-9), and Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS). Responses were linked to inpatient and outpatient

ICD-10 codes from registries. Models were adjusted for age, sex, comorbidities, and pre-existing diagnoses of mental illness.

Results. Of 63,848 invited participants, 42,253 (66%) responded. The median age was 60 (inter-quartile range 53–68) and 19,032 (45%) were male. Responses during the ﬁrst wave of COVID-19 did not suggest increased stress (OR 0.97; 95% conﬁdence interval [CI], 0.93–1.01; p = 0.28) or anxiety (OR 1.01; 95% CI, 0.96 to 1.05; p = 0.61), but were associated with decreased depression (OR 0.89; 95% CI, 0.85–0.93, p < 0.0001) and increased satisfaction with life (OR 1.12; 95% CI, 1.08–1.16, p < 0.0001). A secondary analysis of repeated measures data showed similar results.

Conclusions. Social restrictions were sufﬁcient to contain the pandemic but did not negatively impact validated measures of mental illness or psychiatric well-being. However, responses to individual questions showed signs of fear and stress. This may represent a normal, rather than pathological, population response to a stressful situation.

Keywords: COVID-19, pandemics, mental health

Background

Beginning in China in December 2019 [1], infections by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) caused a pandemic [2] of the respiratory illness coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) leading to 4,353,434 deaths worldwide as of August 17, 2021 [3]. In response, govern-ments around the world enacted measures ranging from social distancing and quarantine to enforced

curfew. While the impact of quarantine and isola-tion on mental health has been reviewed [4], the population effects of the unprecedented measures enacted have not. Calls for action to report on this aspect of the mental health impact of the pandemic have been published [5, 6].

Following the ﬁrst conﬁrmed SARS-CoV-2 infection in Iceland on February 28, 2020, civil emergency

units.text:
COVID-19 and concurrent social restrictions / T. J. Love et al.

In addition to these population-based studies, effects of the pandemic on the quality of life of subpopulations have been reported. This includes students [48], adolescents [49], and pregnant women [50], which is certainly consistent with an increased mental burden in the younger population. The literature also includes studies on the effect of the pandemic on drinking [51], com-puter use [52], and general distress [53]. While our data certainly support the idea that general distress increased during the pandemic, these ﬁndings should not be taken as evidence that mental illness became more prevalent, but rather as exam-ples of different coping mechanisms during these trying times. Certainly, they stress the importance of using the least restrictive measures possible to contain the pandemic to reduce the need for unde-sirable coping methods.

Strengths and weaknesses of the study war-rant discussion. The population-based, prospective design with a large sample size and high participation rate increase the generalizability of the ﬁndings. We used complete, population level data on previous mental illnesses and comorbidities, allowing us to take these factors into account in our analysis. While the results apply directly to the population over 44 years old, we maintain that due to the greater clinical impact of the virus on older patients the data presented are highly rel-evant and show that this vulnerable age group has done well from a mental health perspective. The similar distribution of age and gender in the study group and the underlying population and the size of the study with 28% of the entire population participating reduce the likelihood of selection bias, but some residual effects cannot be excluded. The use of validated instruments to assess mental illnesses and psychiatric well-being gives us the ability to monitor a large population over time but it must be stressed that questionnaires cannot replace clinical diagnosis. Using the frequency of recorded clinical diagnoses might therefore seem a more accurate method of ascertaining population level changes in mental health. However, as the recommendations regarding personal protec-tion during the pandemic are likely to affect access to healthcare, and by extension the frequency of diagnoses, the use of validated instruments is the most reliable method available. Importantly, the instruments used throughout the study period were designed to measure mental health regard-less of COVID-19, and study materials made no mention of the pandemic. This ensures that men-

846 © 2022 The Association for the Publication of the Journal of Internal Medicine. Journal of Internal Medicine, 2022, 291; 837–848

tal health status was measured in a consistent way in the two periods. While we acknowledge the need to measure the effect of the pandemic directly through targeted questions, this practice may limit the ability of researchers to compare responses to those from previous periods.

The generalizability of our ﬁndings deserves con-sideration. While Iceland is a small, cohesive island nation which might make relatively lax restrictions more successful than they would be in larger, more diverse societies, similar limitations have been applied successfully in other Nordic countries. Therefore, we suggest that the results are generalizable to similarly peaceful, cohesive societies, and that they should be considered every-where. It is also interesting to compare our results to those from New Zealand, a homogenous island nation, where harsh restrictions including lockdowns may have resulted in a more pronounced effect on mental health [54]. This lends support to the idea that by using less restrictive measures, it may be possible to reach the desired effect on the spread of the pandemic without a pronounced effect on mental health.

In summary, in this prospective population-based study on the effect of a pandemic and enacted restriction on population mental health, we found no detrimental population level effects on validated measures of symptoms of mental illnesses and psychiatric well-being during the ﬁrst wave of the COVID-19 pandemic. However, responses to individual questions showed signs of fear and stress in the population. The containment measures enacted in the ﬁrst wave of COVID-19 in Iceland were sufﬁcient to contain the pandemic without a detectable negative impact on population level mental health. The most important clinical implication of these ﬁndings is that since the pandemic had no negative effect on the mental health of the adult population at greatest risk of severe COVID-19, and had some positive effects, clinicians should not consider this group vulnerable with regard to mental health due to the pandemic. Further studies are needed to determine the long-term effect of the pandemic on population level mental health.

COVID-19 and concurrent social restrictions / T. J. Love et al.

plans were activated on March 6, 2020. Subse-quently, restrictions on gatherings and public life were enacted in steps and then lifted in phases beginning May 4, 2020, as the ﬁrst wave of the epi-demic drew to a close. By implementing easy access to testing and random population screening as well as a detailed contact tracing program, Iceland had one of the highest rates of COVID-19 testing per capita in the world [7]. The number of new daily infections peaked on March 28, 2020 with a 7-day incidence rate of 117 cases per 100,000, and the number of simultaneously active cases peaked at 299 per 100,000 inhabitants on April 5, 2020. The number of daily new infections then fell rapidly and reached zero for the ﬁrst time on April 23, 2020. When lifting restrictions on public life began on May 4, 2020, the incidence was 0.6 new cases per week per 100,000. Few restrictions remained until the beginning of the next wave on July 22, 2020.

The “Iceland Screens, Treats or Prevents Multiple Myeloma” (iStopMM) study (ClinicalTrials.gov Identiﬁer: NCT03327597) is a population-based screening study for monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined signiﬁcance (MGUS) and a randomized controlled trial of follow-up strategies [8]. The project gathers data on physical and mental illnesses using registries and validated instruments.

Here, we provide population data based on validated instruments designed to evaluate the severity of symptoms associated with two forms of mental illness as well as perceived stress and satisfaction with life before and during the ﬁrst 7 weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic in Iceland. Importantly, we can adjust our models for previously diagnosed mental illness as well as the presence of comorbidities reported to be associated with worse outcomes in COVID-19. The primary goal is to examine the impact of restrictions imposed by authorities on mental illnesses and psychiatric well-being and to understand the role of underlying comorbidities and mental health issues.

Methods

We performed a nested cross-sectional cohort study within iStopMM, with a secondary longitudinal analysis of the subset of participants who had responded in both the unexposed and exposed periods. The data come from iStopMM, a population-based screening study for MGUS and a randomized controlled trial of follow-up strate-

838 © 2022 The Association for the Publication of the Journal of Internal Medicine. Journal of Internal Medicine, 2022, 291; 837–848

gies that began in 2016 (ClinicalTrials.gov Identiﬁer: NCT03327597). All 148,704 individuals in Iceland born in 1975 or earlier received a letter inviting them to participate. Participation is based on informed consent, and data are stored using encrypted identiﬁers. A total of 80,759 (54%) provided informed consent to participate in the study.

While the main outcome measure of iStopMM is the effect of early detection and treatment of multiple myeloma precursor on survival, a secondary goal is to understand the mental health effects associated with screening an entire population for a cancer precursor. Beginning in 2018, we sent out questionnaires daily to individuals randomly selected from the nearly 60,000 participants, excluding those patients who have been randomized for follow-up in iStopMM. The most recent response available from each individual was used for our primary outcome measures.

The iStopMM trial was approved by the Icelandic National Bioethics Committee in April 2016 (VSN 016–22) and an amendment to allow the explo-ration of the effect of COVID-19 in a nested study was approved in April 2020 (VSN 016-22-V18)

Instruments

We used four instruments which have all been applied internationally and validated in Iceland. The Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-7) is a seven-item self-report scale scoring each item from 0 (“not at all”) to 3 (“nearly every day”) and is considered a valid and efﬁcient tool for GAD and for assessing its severity in clinical practice and research. It has good to excellent internal consistency, test–retest reliability, criterion validity, and construct validity. The Icelandic translation of the GAD-7 has good internal consistency with a Cronbach’s α of 0.88 [9–12]. The Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) is a nine-item self-report questionnaire, which scores each of the 9 DSM-IV criteria for diagnosis of depression as 0 (“not at all”) to 3 (“nearly every day”). It has good internal consistency and test–retest reliability along with good criterion and construct validity. Psychometric properties of the Icelandic PHQ-9 have been evaluated with a Cronbach’s α of 0.84 [13–15]. The Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) is a 10-item scale that assesses psychological stress, scoring each item on a ﬁve-point Likert scale from 0 (“never”) to 4 (“very often”). Acceptable psychometric properties of the PSS-10 have been established in various settings.

COVID-19 and concurrent social restrictions / T. J. Love et al.

The Icelandic version has been tested and had a Cronbach’s α of 0.87 [16–19]. The Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) is a ﬁve-item self-report measure scoring each item from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 7 (“strongly agree”) to assess global life satisfaction that has good internal consistency, test– retest reliability, and construct validity. A study of a population-based sample concluded that the Icelandic version of SWLS is a reliable and valid measure of life satisfaction with a Cronbach’s α of 0.87 [20–23]. Of these four instruments, two correlate well with clinical diagnosis of mental illnesses: PHQ-9 with depression and GAD-7 with anxiety disorders [24]. The other two instruments, the PSS-10 [16] and the SWLS [20], measure sub-jective experiences of stress and satisfaction with life. While the latter correlate with general psychiatric well-being, they are not considered proxies for speciﬁc mental illnesses.

Finally, participants were asked to answer two self-report questions with responses on a scale from 1 to 10: “On the whole, how happy do you consider yourself to be?” and “How worried are you about your health?”

Linked data

Data on ICD-10 diagnostic codes for all participants were obtained from registries maintained by the Icelandic Directorate of Health. The registries include information on in- and outpatient encounters in the whole country. Inpatient data are available from 1999, and primary care and hospital outpatient data are available from 2004 and 2010, respectively. Data on cancer diagnoses were obtained from the Icelandic Cancer Registry, which includes all cancers diagnosed in Iceland with mandatory reporting from all doctors and pathologists since 1955, resulting in a near complete registry with high diagnostic accuracy and timeliness [25]. We linked all these data sources to the results from the instruments to provide covariates on prior physical and mental illnesses.

Study and exposure periods

The study period was from October 17, 2018 to May 4, 2020. Exposed individuals were those who provided responses to the instruments during the period beginning with Iceland’s ﬁrst conﬁrmed COVID-19 case on February 28, 2020 and last-ing to the end of the study period. We deﬁned those who responded in the period before the ﬁrst COVID-19 case as unexposed.

Outcomes

Outcomes were deﬁned as a movement between severity categories, scored and partitioned in accordance with published methods [12, 16, 26, 27]. There were four categories for anxiety measured by GAD-7 (none <5/mild 5–9/moderate 10–14/severe >14), ﬁve for depression measured by PHQ-9 (none <5/mild 5–9/moderate 10– 14/moderate-severe 15–19/severe >19), and three for stress measured by PSS-10 (low <14/moderate 14–26/high >26). In the case of SWLS, there were six categories (extreme dissatisfaction <9/dissatisfaction 10–14/slight dissatisfaction 15–19/slight satisfaction 21–25/satisfaction 26– 30/extreme satisfaction >30). We performed a sub-analysis where we used the response to each question comprising the validated instruments. Movement between the steps of the rating scale in each question within the instruments and in the two questions that were not within the instruments was considered a change.

Covariates and stratiﬁcation

Every in- and outpatient ICD-10 diagnostic code for all participants from January 1, 2004 up to and including March 31, 2019 was used to identify the comorbidities previously reported to increase the risk of death from COVID-19: asthma, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, lung disease, cancer, and renal disease [28, 29]. Any past occurrence of one of these codes was considered sufﬁcient for classiﬁcation of a comorbidity. Similarly, ICD-10 codes were used to identify individuals with previous diagnoses of mental illnesses, classiﬁed as F00-F99 and these codes were then manually reviewed to create groupings iden-tifying depression, anxiety, stress disorders, and sleep disturbances. The presence of a single ICD- 10 code occurring in the 2 years prior to respond-ing to the instrument was considered sufﬁcient for classiﬁcation of a mental illness.

Secondary analysis

For individuals with responses at more than one time point, only the most recent response was used for the main analysis so that only one response was included for each participant. Individuals with responses available both before and during the pandemic were included in a secondary analysis comparing the pre-pandemic and during pandemic responses within the same group of individuals.

Statistical analysis

Pearson’s chi-squared test was used to compare the raw rates of moderate to high/severe stress, anxiety, and depression symptoms as well as dissatisfaction with life before and during COVID. To measure changes in the instrument scores, we conducted an ordinal regression analysis to evaluate the odds of moving up one severity category, for example moving from low to moderate stress or from moderate to severe depression. Ordinal regression was also used to evaluate the odds of moving between steps of the rating scale for each individual question on the instruments and between each of the 10 steps of the happiness

and worry questions, which do not have published cut-offs. We calculated the odds ratio (OR) as an approximation of the relative risk along with the 95% conﬁdence interval (CI) for moving between steps between the two time periods. The Brant test [30] was used to evaluate all ordinal regression models for the proportional odds assumption of ordinal regression. Analyses were performed with and without adjustment for age, sex, diagnosis of previous mental illnesses, and those diseases identiﬁed by the World Health Organization to be associated with greater risk of severe course of COVID-19. Stratiﬁed analysis of each category of comorbidity and mental illness was performed as

The secondary analysis was restricted to individuals with responses available both before and during the pandemic and was performed using a generalized estimation equation for an ordinal model to account for repeated measures [31]. All analyses were performed using R v3.6.0.

Results

The iStopMM study has 80,759 consented participants representing 54% of the eligible population, of whom 63,848 provided email addresses and had not been randomized for follow up of MGUS making them eligible for this study. Responses to instruments were received over a period of 565 days from October 17, 2018 to May 4, 2020. Responses were received from 42,253 individuals (66.2%) with responses on two occasions from 12,755 individuals and on three occasions from 595 individuals. The number of responses received in a single day ranged from zero to 898. A total of 32,688 and 23,510 responses were received before and after the ﬁrst case of COVID-19 in Iceland, respectively. Table 1 shows demographic and comorbidity information for all respondents, as well as for those who did not respond. The median age (and proportion of females) among responders, non-responders, and the underlying population was 60 (55%), 60 (55%), and 58 (51%), respectively.

Validated instruments

Moderate to high stress using a PSS-10 score over 13 was reported by 34.9% before and 34.0% (p = 0.049) after the ﬁrst diagnosed COVID-19 case on February 28, moderate to severe anxiety

using a GAD-7 score over 9 by 6.2% and 5.4% (p = 0.001), moderate to severe depression using a PHQ-9 score over 9 by 12.2% and 10.6% (p < 0.001), and dissatisfaction using a SWLS score of less than 20 by 12.4% and 10.1% (p < 0.001). Figure 1 shows these changes in more detail. The OR for moving to a higher (worse) category within each instrument was calculated and the results are summarized in Table 2. The fully adjusted model showed unchanged stress and anxiety, reduced depression, and increased satisfaction with life. The 10-point happiness scale showed increased happiness, and the health worry scale showed an increased level of health-related worry. Ordinal regression models met the proportional odds assumption as tested by the Brant test.

Individual questions

While the PSS-10 instrument as a whole did not indicate there was an increase in population level stress, two of the questions showed increased stress during the ﬁrst wave of COVID-19, opposite to the total calculated score; “…how often have you been upset because of something that happened unexpectedly?” with an OR of 1.31 (1.26–1.35, p < 0.001) and “…how often have you felt that you were unable to control the important things in your life?” with an OR of 1.27 (1.23–1.32, p < 0.001). One question on the GAD-7 instrument pointed to an increase in anxiety, with an OR of 1.52 (1.45–1.59, p < 0.001) for the question “…Feeling afraid as if something awful might happen.” The questions “Little interest or pleasure in doing things?” and “Trouble concentrating on things…” on the PHQ-9 instrument moved in a direction opposite to that of the whole with ORs of 1.08 (1.04–1.12, p = 0.0001) and 1.06 (1.01–1.10,

Conclusions

In this prospective, population-based cohort nested in a randomized screening study, we found no evidence of increased levels of mental illnesses or deterioration in psychiatric well-being at the population level during the ﬁrst wave of COVID-19 in Iceland using responses to validated instruments returned by more than 40,000 participants, representing a response rate over 66%. While individual questions indicate the population was more likely to worry about their health, feel afraid, be upset about unexpected events, and experience a sense of inability to control important aspects of their lives, these changes did not translate into clinically important change for the worse. On the contrary, the SWLS measured an increased level of satisfaction with life among the population. This is

COVID-19 and concurrent social restrictions / T. J. Love et al.

to our knowledge the ﬁrst population-based study to use the same validated instruments to compare the mental health status of the general population before and during a wave of the pandemic.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to the restriction of individual freedoms for the beneﬁt of population health, with a focus on protecting vulnerable populations. There is substantial inter-country variability regarding the particulars of restrictions and their enforcement [32], giving reason to compare the effectiveness and potential detrimental effects of various measures between countries. Brieﬂy, the restrictions enacted in Iceland were based on recommendations by infectious disease experts and involved social distancing, limitations on the size of gatherings, and the forced closure of some types of businesses. However, there were no lockdowns or curfews, and restaurants as well as schools for students up to 16 years of age remained open throughout the study period. These measures appear to have struck a balance between being adequate to suppress the spread of infection while not so onerous as to impact the mental health of the general population.

Our unique comparison data including the period immediately preceding the pandemic allow us to expand on the previous literature by showing that there was no increase in the rate of moderate to severe symptoms of depression, stress, and anxiety among the general population during the ﬁrst wave of COVID-19 in Iceland. The absolute rates we found are comparable to those described previously in other populations, supporting the generalizability of our ﬁndings [13, 33, 34].

The literature on the mental health impact of the COVID-19 pandemic is not mature, and we were unable to ﬁnd reviews of the literature that went beyond describing the point prevalence of mental illnesses during the pandemic. We have found few studies with granular data on mental illness in large populations using the same methods before and during COVID-19, and none that adjust for the effects of comorbidities and exist-ing mental health diagnoses. One online survey of 2025 adults from the United Kingdom found higher levels of anxiety and depression compared to historical controls, but “… not dramatically so” [35]. Two published studies based on the same dataset from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (UKHLS) found that an increased proportion of the population had scores on the General Health

Questionnaire (GHQ-12) indicative of a “…poten-tially clinically signiﬁcant level of mental distress” [36, 37]. Finally, a study from Germany found that the population was “…largely resilient to the immediate effects of lockdown on mental health…” [38] These ﬁndings agree with our observation that there were individual questions that suggested a marked effect of the pandemic. However, it is important to note that our results neither reach the threshold of suggesting an increased prevalence of mental illness, nor do they suggest an increased severity of symptoms suggestive of mental illness. On the contrary, these ﬁndings may represent a healthy response to a crisis. Such a response may be necessary so that individuals will feel the need to take necessary precautions to protect their health. However, future studies will be needed to shed light on the effect of extended or repeated periods of such stressors on mental health.

A recent paper attempted to estimate the global burden of mental illness during the pandemic across 204 countries by using a Global Burden of Disease (GBD) model to extrapolate the best available data from 16 countries [39]. The supplemen-tary material reveals 47 data sources with vary-ing inclusion methods, comparison groups, and methods, including the use of market research data, with the majority based on less than 1500 participants. The resulting GBD model is complex and impressive, but as the accompanying editorial points out it has signiﬁcant shortcomings, including predictions for some countries that are contra-dicted by real-world data [40]. The comments in the editorial furthermore echo what we have stated here, i.e. that responses showing an increased anxiety on GAD-7 would “… not be unreasonable …” in the context of COVID-19 and might not indicate the presence of an anxiety disorder. Of note, half of the individuals included in the GBD model came from one German study with 113,928 participants, where an increase in anxiety and depression was only observed among those less than 50 years of age [41]. This is consistent with studies from the United States [42], Spain [43], Canada [44], and the Netherlands [45] highlighted in a JAMA view-point article [46]. It may seem counterintuitive that younger individuals are at greater risk for mental health decline during the pandemic consider-ing the risk of severe COVID-19 increases with age. However, as mental health resilience increases with age [47], it is possible that restrictions on freedoms associated with COVID-19 affect young peo-ple disproportionately.
